title: Lucifer and Satan as distinct figures
statement: Lucifer and Satan are distinct: biblically, 'Lucifer' renders helel ben shahar, a taunt against the king of Babylon in Isaiah 14 with no Devil in the passage, while ha-satan in Job and Zechariah is a courtroom role in the divine council; their fusion into a single Devil is a datable Second Temple-to-Christian development sealed in the Anglophone imagination by Milton; and in the canon the two are distinct individuals on opposite sides of the conflict — Lucifer the exiled-creator faction leader, Satan the home-world opposition leader.

includes: The biblical non-identity layer, which is mainstream-supportable: Isaiah 14's helel ben shahar as royal taunt; ha-satan as adversarial court functionary in Job 1-2 and Zechariah 3; the fusion as reception history (Second Temple development through patristic consolidation to Milton)

The canonical layer, which is framework: Lucifer as leader of the exiled-creator faction (the Eden disclosure and exile), Satan as leader of the home-world opposition that distrusts humanity — two individuals, opposed factions, neither a devil
The consequence for corpus prose: pages must not merge the two figures, and must not read biblical satan-passages as Lucifer material or vice versa without the record's mapping stated
excludes: Lucifer-Satan identity in any layer, which the record exists to deny
Any claim that the biblical authors knew the canon's two-figure account; the canonical mapping is supplied by the framework
The theology of a cosmic Devil; the record concerns two named figures and a documented fusion
Etymological claims beyond the Vulgate rendering history of helel ben shahar

source_references.locator: Chapters 2-3: the Serpent faction, its Eden disclosure and exile (Lucifer); Satan's opposition role and the Council; Satan and the testing of Job
Isaiah 14:12-15 (helel ben shahar, the taunt against the king of Babylon)
Job 1-2 (ha-satan among the benei ha-elohim; the commissioned testing)
The adversary role in the heavenly court — the standard treatment of ha-satan as function rather than name
The social history of Satan's development in the Second Temple and early Christian period
The combat-myth genealogy of the Devil figure

alternatives.statement: The traditional fusion, though late, tracks a real theological unity in the material; the distinction is antiquarian rather than substantive.
Both names are literary figures within their own genres (taunt-song; court narrative); neither refers to any individual, so the canon's mapping has nothing to attach to.
The canon's two figures and the two biblical figures are independent pairs that the corpus aligns; the alignment is supplied by the framework, not by the texts.
